caption:
Is the Pont du Gard held together with mortar? No. It was built largely without mortar or clamps — 50,400 tons of limestone, some blocks weighing 6 tons, cut so precisely they hold by friction and gravity alone.

The bridge is 49 m high and 274 m long, carrying water 50 km to Roman N\u00eemes. Its gradient is absurd: the Pont du Gard itself drops 2.5 cm over 456 m. Between the bridge and St Bonnet the engineers had to allow a fall of 7 mm per 100 m.

Builders numbered the blocks and inscribed instructions on them — fronte dextra, fronte sinistra, front right, front left. About 800 to 1,000 workers, roughly fifteen years.

The top levels curve upstream. For a long time this was read as clever engineering against the river. A microtopographic survey in 1989 found the cause: the stone expands and contracts about 5 mm a day in the sun, and centuries of that produced the bend.

It survived because it was useful. From the 13th century the seigneurs, later the Bishops of Uz\u00e8s, levied tolls and kept it repaired. The worst damage was French, not barbarian: in the 1620s the Duke of Rohan cut away one side of the second tier to a third of its thickness to move artillery across.

Still open: who built it and when. Credit long went to Agrippa around 19 BC, but coins in the N\u00eemes outflow are no older than Claudius, and newer excavation points to 40\u201360 AD.

Images: an album photograph once owned by Paul-Jean Toulet; Dominique Roman's 1860 view; an anonymous postcard, c.1900\u20131910; Cl\u00e9risseau's 1804 engraving; Hubert Robert's 1787 painting; and a 2012 photograph of the river beach downstream.
